newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Agency raises Dutch 1996 GDP growth forecast.
newsitem.headline: Agency raises Dutch 1996 GDP growth forecast.

text.p: The Dutch planning agency Centraal Planbureau (CPB) said on Wednesday it had raised its forecast for Dutch 1996 Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth to 2.75 percent from a previously expected 2.5 percent.
It added this was mainly caused by increasing consumer spending.
"In September we expected a (full-year) consumer spending growth of two percent, but now we see a three percent increase," a CPB spokesman told Reuters.
The bureau maintained its 1997 GDP growth forecast of 2.75 percent.

"Although inflation has been accelerating since October, the 1996 rise of the CPI (consumer price index) will turn out to be a modest two percent, slightly down from the previous forecast," the CPB said.
Previously, it expected the 1996 CPI to show a 2.25 percent rise. The bureau maintained its forecast that Dutch consumer prices are expected to rise by 2.5 percent in 1997.

The CPB said the expected 1996 and 1997 GDP growth for the Netherlands was favorable compared with other European Union (EU) countries, where average growth figures of 1.5 and 2.25 percent respectively are seen for these years.
"The growth differential with the EU increases further," the planning agency said.

It expects Dutch consumer spending growth to slow to two percent next year from three percent in 1996. The number of jobs is seen rising by about two percent in 1997 but as the supply side of the Dutch labour market will also grow the overall effect on unemployment figures is expected to remain limited.
The Dutch state's total tax income in both 1996 and 1997 is now expected to be more than two billion guilders higher than previous forecasts indicated.

Higher oil prices will add an extra 1.5 billion guilders to natural gas revenues, which are linked to the oil price, next year. But the agency warned that unemployment benefits are expected to be higher in 1997 than previously expected.
"Still, the general government deficit, and hence the public debt/GDP ratio, is coming down faster than projected last September," the CPB said.
